key_terms.meaning: Converts analyte concentration into an electrical signal using a recognition layer and a transducer.
The chemical or biological species whose concentration is being measured.
Chemical sensor with a biological recognition element such as an enzyme, antibody or DNA probe.
Measures analyte through an equilibrium EMF at near-zero current; output follows the Nernst relation.
Measures analyte through a current at fixed applied potential; current is proportional to reaction rate.
Metal-oxide film whose resistance changes when a reducing or oxidising gas adsorbs on its surface.
Electrochemical or solid-electrolyte cell that gives a current or EMF set by oxygen partial pressure.
Ratio of water-vapour pressure in air to saturation vapour pressure at the same temperature, in percent.
Temperature at which air becomes saturated and water vapour starts to condense at constant pressure.
Gas sensor in which a semiconductor film, often SnO₂, changes conductance when gas adsorbs.
Resistor whose resistance changes with mechanical strain, used in silicon diaphragms and cantilevers.
Thin membrane that deflects under pressure; deflection or strain is read by piezoresistors or capacitance.
Etching deep into a silicon wafer to form cavities, diaphragms, beams or channels.
Package with sensing element, signal conditioning, processor and digital interface giving calibrated addressed output.
Sensor built on a bendable substrate so it can conform to skin, cloth or curved machinery.
Combining readings from several sensors by rules or estimation to reduce uncertainty and fill gaps.
Ionic conductor that carries one mobile ion and blocks electrons, used in Nernst-type cells.
Piezoelectric delay line whose wave velocity or amplitude shifts when mass or elasticity changes on its surface.
Biosensor using an enzyme to convert a target into a product that the transducer detects.
Ion-sensitive field-effect transistor; gate insulator exposed to solution makes drain current depend on ion activity.
Platinum cathode behind an oxygen-permeable membrane, held near −0.6 V; its current is proportional to blood pO₂.
Threshold shift per pH: ideally 2.303 kT/q, 59 mV at 25 °C and 61.5 mV at 37 °C; nitride gates come close.
Small redox molecule (ferrocene, ferricyanide) that carries electrons from the enzyme to the electrode at a low potential.

takeaways: A chemical sensor has recognition plus transduction; a biosensor adds a biological recognition element in front of the same transducers.
Electrochemical sensors split into potentiometric EMF, amperometric current and conductometric conductance, chosen by the analyte reaction.
Gas sensors use resistance, current or EMF; selectivity depends on material, temperature and a filter or reference electrode.
Humidity is reported as relative humidity at a stated temperature because saturation vapour pressure changes strongly with temperature.
In a semiconductor sensor the material is the transducer, so doping, grain size and operating temperature set sensitivity and drift.
MEMS micromachining makes diaphragms, beams and channels on silicon, read by piezoresistors, capacitors or heaters.
A smart sensor outputs a calibrated digital value because signal conditioning and a processor sit inside the same package.
Flexible sensors conform to curved surfaces, and fusion of several readings improves estimates when each sensor has different errors.
A solid electrolyte gives a Nernst EMF for the ion it conducts; a SAW device senses mass or elasticity change on a piezoelectric surface.
Biosensors are named on two axes, biological element and transducer, with ISFET, IMFET and the glucose strip as standard exam cases.

In medicine the same sensors become the glucose meter, the blood-gas analyser (Clark pO₂, ISFET pH), the anaesthesia oxygen monitor, the arterial-line pressure transducer and the ventilator humidifier and flow sensor.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask for a block diagram, a classification, one working principle with formula, and two applications or limitations, so prepare side-by-side comparisons of transducer classes. Biomedical syllabi stress biosensors: their advantages and limitations, components, classification by transduction (electrochemical, optical, acoustic, calorimetric) and by biological element (enzyme, immunosensor), the ISFET and IMFET, and blood glucose sensors.

bank.q: Define chemical sensor and biosensor. Draw the block diagram of a biosensor and classify biosensors by transducer, giving one example for each class.
outline: clear definitions of chemical sensor and biosensor
diagram with bioreceptor, transducer and signal conditioning
electrochemical, optical, acoustic and calorimetric classes
one example per class and the two-axis naming rule
answer: Chemical sensor. A device that turns the concentration (or activity) of one chemical species, the analyte, into an electrical signal. It has a recognition layer that interacts with the analyte and a transducer that converts that interaction into a voltage, current, resistance, frequency or light level. A SnO₂ gas resistor and a glass pH electrode are chemical sensors.

Biosensor. A chemical sensor whose recognition layer is biological: an enzyme, antibody, nucleic acid (DNA or aptamer), whole cell or tissue. The biology gives selectivity that a bare transducer lacks; the transducer gives a number. The glucose strip, an enzyme with an amperometric electrode, is the standard example.

answer.text: Block diagram. The signal passes through five blocks in series:
answer.pre:
analyte (sample) → bio-recognition element → transducer → signal conditioning → display / data
  glucose in blood → glucose oxidase → Pt electrode at +0.6 V → current-to-voltage, filter, ADC → mmol/L

answer: Each block has one job. The bio element reacts only with its target and produces something the transducer can see (here H₂O₂). The transducer converts it to an electrical quantity (here a current proportional to the H₂O₂). Conditioning amplifies, filters, linearises and applies the calibration. The display gives the concentration with its unit.

answer.text: Classification by transducer, with one example each.

head: Class
What is measured
Example
rows: current at a fixed electrode potential
pH glass electrode; ISFET; urea EnFET
heat of reaction, as a temperature rise
enzyme thermistor for glucose or urea

answer: Classification by biological element. Enzyme sensors (glucose oxidase, urease, lactate oxidase), immunosensors (antibody and antigen), nucleic-acid sensors (DNA probes, aptamers), and whole-cell or tissue sensors (bacteria for BOD and toxicity). These are catalytic (enzyme, cell: the target is converted and the sensor can be reused) or affinity (antibody, DNA: the target is bound, usually single-use).

Two-axis naming rule. Every biosensor is named by element and transducer together: enzyme + amperometric = glucose strip; antibody + optical = SPR immunosensor; enzyme + FET = EnFET; antibody + FET = IMFET. An open question should be answered on both axes.

Advantages and limitations. Advantages: high selectivity from the biology, a small sample (one drop), fast response, low cost per test, and use at the bedside. Limitations: the biological layer denatures, so shelf life is months; response depends on temperature and pH; electrodes foul; and each batch needs calibration.
Calibration in numbers. A linear sensor obeys I = I₀ + S C. Standards of 2.0 and 10.0 mmol/L giving 45 and 165 nA fix S = (165 − 45)/(10.0 − 2.0) = 15 nA per mmol/L and I₀ = 45 − 15 × 2.0 = 15 nA.
Check. A sample current of 120 nA gives C = (120 − 15)/15 = 7.0 mmol/L = 126 mg/dL; putting C = 7.0 back gives 15 + 15 × 7.0 = 120 nA, as read.

bank.q: Explain potentiometric and amperometric transduction in electrochemical sensors. State the measured quantity, the driving circuit and one interference for each.
outline: potentiometric measures EMF at near-zero current
amperometric measures current at fixed potential
reference electrode and three-electrode cell roles
interferences and selectivity limits
answer: Potentiometric transduction. The sensing electrode and a reference electrode stand in the solution, and the EMF between them is measured with (ideally) no current flowing. The EMF follows the Nernst relation: E = E₀ + (2.303 RT / zF) log₁₀ a, where a is the ion activity and z its charge. For a singly charged ion at 25 °C the slope is 2.303 × 8.314 × 298.15 / 96 485 = 59.2 mV per decade.

Measured quantity and circuit. The quantity is a voltage that grows with the logarithm of activity. A glass pH electrode has a resistance of 10⁸ Ω or more, so the meter must have an input resistance far above that, 10¹² Ω or more (an electrometer or FET-input op-amp buffer). Drawing current would polarise the electrode and change the reading. A stable reference electrode, Ag/AgCl or calomel, fixes the other half of the cell.

Interference, potentiometric. Other ions also reach the membrane. A glass electrode responds to Na⁺ at high pH (the alkaline error), and an ion-selective electrode is described by the Nikolsky equation with a selectivity coefficient for each interfering ion. Temperature changes the slope (57.2 mV/pH at 15 °C, 59.2 at 25 °C), so the meter needs temperature compensation.

Amperometric transduction. The working electrode is held at a fixed potential at which the analyte (or a product of its reaction) is oxidised or reduced, and the current is measured. When the reaction is limited by diffusion to the electrode, the current is proportional to concentration: I = I₀ + S C.

answer.text: Circuit: the three-electrode potentiostat. The working electrode carries the reaction; the reference electrode senses the solution potential and carries no current; the counter electrode supplies the current. An op-amp drives the counter electrode so that working-to-reference voltage equals the set value, and a transimpedance amplifier turns the working current into a voltage:
answer.pre:
V<sub>out</sub> = − I R<sub>f</sub>
120 nA through R<sub>f</sub> = 10 MΩ gives V<sub>out</sub> = −1.2 V

answer: Interference, amperometric. Any species that reacts at the chosen potential adds current. On a first-generation glucose electrode at +0.6 to +0.7 V, ascorbic acid, uric acid and paracetamol all oxidise and read as glucose. Remedies are a lower potential (a mediator at +0.2 to +0.4 V), a permselective membrane, or a blank electrode without enzyme whose current is subtracted. Dissolved oxygen also varies, which changes the first-generation response.

answer.text: Side-by-side.

answer: Check. pH 7 to pH 8 is a tenfold fall in H⁺ and moves a glass electrode by 59.2 mV at 25 °C; on the amperometric sensor above, raising glucose from 2.0 to 10.0 mmol/L moves the current from 45 to 165 nA, a factor of 3.7 for a factor of 5 in concentration, because of the 15 nA blank.

bank.q: Describe an oxygen sensor and a hydrogen sensor. Compare their output type, operating temperature and main cross-sensitivity.
outline: oxygen sensor as electrochemical or solid-electrolyte cell
hydrogen sensor as catalytic, metal-oxide or electrochemical device
output is current, resistance or EMF
cross-sensitivity to humidity or other gases
answer: Oxygen sensor, the zirconia (Nernst) cell. A tube or disc of yttria-stabilised zirconia (YSZ) with porous platinum electrodes on both faces. One face sees reference air (20.9 % O₂), the other the sample. Above about 350 °C the ceramic conducts O²⁻ ions, so practical cells are heated to 600 to 800 °C. Oxygen is reduced on the oxygen-rich side (O₂ + 4e⁻ → 2O²⁻), the ions cross, and the cell gives E = (RT/4F) ln(p₁/p₂).

Worked value. At 973 K with 20.9 % and 2.0 % O₂: RT/4F = 8.314 × 973 / (4 × 96 485) = 20.96 mV, ln 10.45 = 2.347, so E = 49.2 mV with the reference side positive. A limiting-current version with a diffusion hole gives a current linear in O₂ instead; a paramagnetic analyser uses the magnetic pull on O₂ and reads percent oxygen linearly, as in anaesthesia machines; the Clark electrode measures blood pO₂ amperometrically.

Hydrogen sensors. (1) Palladium devices: a Pd film changes resistance, a Pd-gate MOSFET shifts its threshold, or a Pd/Si Schottky diode lowers its barrier as hydrogen dissolves in the palladium; they work near 100 °C and detect ppm levels. (2) Catalytic pellistor: two beads at about 500 °C in a Wheatstone bridge, one with a Pt or Pd catalyst; hydrogen burns on the active bead, its coil resistance rises and the bridge gives a voltage proportional to the heat of combustion, read in % LEL. (3) Thermal conductivity cell: hydrogen conducts heat about seven times better than air, so a heated wire runs cooler and its resistance falls.

answer.text: Comparison.

head: Property
Zirconia O₂ cell
Pellistor (H₂ and other fuels)
Pd MOSFET (H₂)
rows: reducing gases burn on hot Pt and lower the local O₂
every combustible gas; poisoned by silicones and lead
other hydrogen-bearing gases; poisoned by H₂S

answer: Output type. The zirconia cell is a voltage source with a logarithmic law; a tenfold change in oxygen at 973 K moves E by 20.96 × ln 10 = 48.3 mV, so it suits the narrow band around stoichiometric combustion. The pellistor and thermal-conductivity cell are resistance changes read by a bridge, linear over their range. Palladium devices give a voltage shift that saturates at high hydrogen.

Operating temperature in practice. The zirconia cell is useless cold because its ionic conductivity follows σ₀ exp(−Ea/kT); the pellistor must be hot enough to burn the gas; the palladium devices are the only ones near room temperature, which suits battery-powered leak detectors.

Cross-sensitivity in practice. A zirconia cell in a fuel-rich exhaust sees CO and H₂ burn on its platinum, which is why it switches sharply at stoichiometry. A pellistor cannot tell hydrogen from methane, so it reads total combustibles. A thermal-conductivity hydrogen cell is upset by helium (which also conducts well) and CO₂.
Check. With 1.0 % O₂ in the sample at 1073 K, E = 23.12 mV × ln 20.9 = 23.12 × 3.040 = 70.3 mV: lower oxygen and higher temperature both raise the EMF, as the formula predicts.

bank.q: Explain three humidity sensor methods: capacitive, resistive and dew-point. Why must relative humidity be quoted with temperature?
outline: capacitive sensor uses dielectric change of polymer or oxide
resistive sensor uses conductivity change in a hygroscopic film
dew-point sensor cools a mirror until condensation
relative humidity depends on saturation vapour pressure at that temperature
answer: Definitions first. RH = 100 × pv / psat(T), where pv is the water vapour pressure and psat(T) the saturation vapour pressure at the air temperature. Dew point is the temperature at which psat equals pv.

Capacitive sensor. A thin hygroscopic polymer (polyimide) or porous Al2O3 film between two electrodes, the top one porous so vapour can enter. Dry polymer has εr ≈ 3 and water εr ≈ 80, so absorbed water raises the effective permittivity and C = εr ε0 A/d rises almost linearly with RH between 20 and 80 %. It is read with AC near 1 kHz, often in an oscillator or switched-capacitor circuit. Worked value: 100 pF at 20 % and 160 pF at 80 % give 1 pF per %RH and an intercept of 80 pF, so 145 pF means 65 % RH.

Resistive sensor. A porous ceramic (Al2O3, TiO2) or a polymer electrolyte between interdigitated electrodes. Water adsorbed on the pore walls dissociates into ions and conducts, so the resistance falls by orders of magnitude from dry to wet, roughly exponentially with RH. It must be read with AC: DC would electrolyse the water film and polarise the material. It is cheap but less linear and slower than the capacitive type, and may need periodic heating to clean the surface.

Dew-point (chilled mirror) hygrometer. A small mirror on a Peltier cooler is lit by an LED and watched by a photodetector. The controller cools the mirror until dew begins to form and scatters the light, then holds the mirror at the temperature where the dew neither grows nor shrinks; a platinum resistance thermometer in the mirror reads that dew point. It is a primary method with no polymer calibration, so it is the reference against which capacitive sensors are checked, but it is slow, costly and upset by dirt on the mirror.

answer.text: Comparison.
Why RH must be quoted with temperature. psat rises steeply with temperature, so the same water vapour gives a different RH at a different temperature. Worked case: pv = 1.90 kPa.

answer: The amount of water and the dew point (16.7 °C from the Magnus formula) did not change, yet RH fell from 60.0 % to 33.8 %. A reading of "60 % RH" without its temperature therefore does not say how much water is present or whether a surface will collect dew. In hospitals this matters: an incubator or a ventilator humidifier is controlled on RH at a set temperature.
Check. At the dew point the RH is 100 %: psat(16.7 °C) = 0.6109 exp(17.625 × 16.7 / 259.74) = 0.6109 × 3.10 = 1.90 kPa, equal to pv.

bank.q: What is a semiconductor gas sensor? Explain the roles of material, doping, grain size and heater temperature in SnO₂-type sensors.
outline: surface adsorption changes depletion layer and conductance
material and dopant set selectivity
grain size controls sensitivity
heater temperature controls response and recovery
answer: Definition. A semiconductor gas sensor (chemiresistor) is a heated film or sintered bead of an n-type metal oxide, usually SnO₂, between two electrodes on a ceramic substrate with a heater on the back. A gas that reacts with its surface changes its resistance; the sensitivity is S = Rair / Rgas.

Mechanism. In clean air, oxygen adsorbs on the hot surface and takes electrons from the conduction band, becoming O⁻ or O²⁻. This leaves a depleted layer at every grain surface and a potential barrier at every grain-to-grain contact, so the film resistance is high. A reducing gas such as CO, H₂, LPG or ethanol reacts with the adsorbed oxygen (CO + O⁻ → CO₂ + e⁻) and returns the electrons: the depleted layer thins, the barriers fall and the resistance drops. An oxidising gas such as NO₂ does the opposite and raises the resistance.

Material. The oxide must be a wide-gap semiconductor that is stable in hot air and whose surface exchanges oxygen readily. SnO₂ (gap 3.6 eV) is the standard; ZnO, WO₃ (good for NO₂), TiO₂ and Ga₂O₃ are alternatives, each with a different best gas and temperature.

Doping (catalysts). A small amount of Pd or Pt on the grains speeds the surface reaction and lowers the best working temperature; it also shifts the selectivity, for example Pd towards CO and methane. Bulk dopants such as Sb change the base resistance. A filter layer of charcoal or zeolite in front of the film removes some interfering gases.

answer.text: Grain size. Conduction crosses every grain, so the smaller the grains, the larger the share of the material that is depleted surface. When the grain diameter falls to about twice the depletion depth (a few nanometres for SnO₂), the whole grain is depleted in air and the response rises sharply. The surface-to-volume ratio shows the trend:

answer: Small grains must be kept small: at high temperature they sinter and grow, which is one cause of long-term drift.

Heater temperature. Below about 200 °C the surface reaction is too slow and the sensor barely responds; above about 500 °C the adsorbed oxygen leaves and the response falls again. Each gas has a temperature of peak response, typically 300 to 400 °C for SnO₂, so the heater sets both the speed and the selectivity. Some sensors cycle the heater between two temperatures and read the resistance at each to separate two gases. The heater also costs power, tens to hundreds of milliwatts, which limits battery use.

answer.text: Reading circuit. The film Rs sits in a divider with a load resistor RL on a supply Vc, and an amplifier or comparator watches the load voltage:
answer.pre:
V<sub>out</sub> = V<sub>c</sub> R<sub>L</sub> / (R<sub>s</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>)
V<sub>c</sub> = 5 V, R<sub>L</sub> = 10 kΩ:  air R<sub>s</sub> = 60 kΩ → 0.714 V;  gas R<sub>s</sub> = 4 kΩ → 3.57 V

answer: Limitations. Poor selectivity (a kitchen alarm responds to cooking alcohol as well as LPG), humidity dependence (water also reacts with the surface), drift as grains sinter, and poisoning by silicone vapours.
Check. S = Rair / Rgas = 60 kΩ / 4 kΩ = 15, and the divider output rises by 3.57 / 0.714 = 5.0 times, so the comparator threshold can sit anywhere between them, for example at 2 V.

bank.q: Explain a piezoresistive MEMS pressure sensor with a silicon diaphragm and Wheatstone bridge. Include the pressure-to-strain-to-voltage chain.
outline: pressure deflects diaphragm and creates strain
piezoresistors change resistance
bridge converts resistance change to voltage
sensitivity in mV/V and effects of temperature
answer: Construction. A (100) silicon die is etched from the back in KOH to leave a thin diaphragm, 5 to 25 µm thick, clamped by the thick rim. The die is anodically bonded to a glass base; a sealed vacuum cavity gives an absolute sensor, a hole through the glass a gauge sensor. Four p-type piezoresistors are ion-implanted into the top surface near the clamped edges, where the bending stress is largest, and joined by aluminium tracks into a Wheatstone bridge.

Pressure to stress to strain. A pressure difference P bends the diaphragm. For a clamped plate the surface stress at the edge is roughly proportional to P (a/h)², where a is the side and h the thickness, so a thinner or wider diaphragm is more sensitive but has a lower burst pressure and stays linear over a smaller range (keep deflection below about one fifth of h). The strain at the gauges, ε, follows the stress.

Strain to resistance. Silicon is piezoresistive: strain changes the band structure and the carrier mobility, so ΔR/R = G ε with G between 100 and 200, against about 2 for a metal foil gauge. In p-type silicon the coefficient along the stress and the one across it have opposite signs, so the two gauges lying across the edge rise in resistance and the two lying along it fall.

answer.text: Resistance to voltage: the full bridge. Placing the rising pair in opposite arms gives four active arms:
answer.pre:
V<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>s</sub> (ΔR / R)            (four active arms)
V<sub>o</sub> ≈ V<sub>s</sub> (ΔR / R) / 4        (one active arm)

answer.text: Worked chain. G = 120, strain 2 × 10⁻⁴ at full scale, R = 5 kΩ, Vs = 5 V, full scale 2 bar.

answer: Sensitivity in mV/V. Data sheets quote the output per volt of supply because the bridge output is proportional to Vs; a ratiometric ADC that uses the same supply as its reference then cancels supply changes. Typical parts give 5 to 20 mV/V/bar at full scale.

Temperature effects. Three appear. The zero offset drifts because the four resistors are never exactly matched. The resistance itself rises with temperature (TCR about +0.1 to +0.3 %/K), which the full bridge largely cancels because all four arms move together. The piezoresistive coefficient, and so the span, falls as temperature rises (TCS about −0.2 %/K). A constant-current supply partly compensates the span, and a smart-sensor package corrects both offset and span from an on-chip temperature sensor.

Signal conditioning. 120 mV is too small for a 0 to 5 V ADC, so an instrumentation amplifier with a gain of about 40 follows the bridge, giving 4.8 V at full scale. The same chain is the disposable arterial-line blood-pressure transducer, built to 5 µV/V/mmHg: 3.0 mV at 120 mmHg on 5 V.
Check. At half scale (1 bar) the strain halves, ΔR/R = 0.012 and the full bridge gives 5 × 0.012 = 60 mV, half of 120 mV, which is the linearity the data sheet promises within its stated error.

bank.q: Define a smart sensor. List its internal blocks and explain the functions of calibration, addressing and digital interface.
outline: sensing element plus signal conditioning
processor and memory store calibration
digital interface and address
advantages and limitations in a network
answer: Definition. A smart sensor is a sensing element packaged with its signal conditioning, an analog-to-digital converter, a processor and memory, and a digital interface, so that it delivers a calibrated, addressed reading in engineering units and can check itself. IEEE 1451 adds a Transducer Electronic Data Sheet (TEDS) in that memory.

answer.text: Internal blocks.
answer.pre:
sensing element → amplifier + filter → ADC → microcontroller ↔ memory (coefficients, TEDS) → bus interface
       ↑ on-chip temperature sensor and internal reference feed the microcontroller

answer: Sensing element. The transducer itself, for example a piezoresistive bridge giving 10 mV/kPa. Amplifier and filter. Raise the signal to the ADC range and remove noise outside the band; the analog stage must not clip, because no later correction can recover a clipped signal. ADC. Turns the voltage into a count; a 12-bit converter on 3.3 V has steps of 3.3 / 4096 = 0.806 mV.

Processor and memory. The microcontroller converts counts to the measurand using coefficients stored at factory calibration: offset, gain, a linearity table and temperature coefficients. It also runs self-calibration (switching an internal reference to the input), self-diagnosis (open circuit, overrange, stuck output) and autoranging.

answer.text: Calibration in numbers. A blood-pressure module read 12 counts at 0 kPa and 3712 counts at 40 kPa at 25 °C, and its span falls 0.2 % per °C. In use at 37 °C it reads 1492 counts.

answer: Without the stored temperature coefficient the module would report 120 mmHg, 3 mmHg low; the memory is what makes the correction possible without an outside computer.

Addressing. On a shared bus every sensor has an address, so one master can poll many sensors on two or four wires. I²C uses a 7-bit address (128 codes, of which 112 are usable after the reserved ones); CAN identifies messages by an 11-bit or 29-bit identifier; HART adds a digital address to a 4 to 20 mA loop. TEDS lets the master read each sensor's identity, range and calibration date when it is plugged in, so the network configures itself.

Digital interface. The reading travels as a number with status bits, so cable resistance, pickup and ground loops no longer change it, and the master can read the fault flags. I²C and SPI serve short runs on a board; CAN suits vehicles and some medical equipment; a 4 to 20 mA loop with HART serves long plant cables.

Advantages. Calibration and compensation close to the signal, fewer wires, self-test, interchangeable sensors and remote configuration. Limitations. Higher cost from calibration time, power for the processor, conversion delay, and the false belief that a digital output is accurate: 12 bits fix resolution, not accuracy.

Check. One step of the 12-bit ADC behind a gain of 100 is 0.806 mV / 100 = 8.06 µV at the element; at 10 µV/Pa that is 0.806 Pa per count, so the module above resolves pressure far more finely than its 3 mmHg (400 Pa) temperature error, which is why the correction matters more than extra bits.

bank.q: Explain the Nernst EMF of a solid electrolyte oxygen sensor and the mass-loading principle of a SAW sensor. Compare ISFET and IMFET gates.
outline: solid electrolyte conducts one ion and gives Nernst EMF
SAW velocity or amplitude changes with surface mass
ISFET gate insulator senses ion activity
IMFET adds an immobilised enzyme or antibody layer
answer: Solid electrolyte. A solid that conducts one ion and almost no electrons: yttria-stabilised zirconia conducts O²⁻, Nafion H⁺, sodium beta-alumina Na⁺. Its ionic conductivity follows σ = σ₀ exp(−Ea/kT), so a zirconia cell is useful only above about 350 °C and is run at 600 to 800 °C.

answer.text: Nernst EMF. Two porous platinum electrodes see oxygen partial pressures p₁ (reference) and p₂ (sample). Oxygen is reduced on the rich side (O₂ + 4e⁻ → 2O²⁻), ions cross the electrolyte, and at equilibrium the open-circuit EMF is

answer: The 4 is the four electrons per O₂ molecule. The law is logarithmic, needs a reference gas, and makes the electrode with more oxygen positive. It is the car lambda sensor and the boiler flue analyser.

SAW sensor principle. An interdigital transducer (IDT) on a piezoelectric substrate such as quartz launches a Rayleigh surface wave whose energy lies within about one wavelength of the surface; a second IDT receives it. The finger pitch fixes the wavelength λ, and f = v/λ.

answer.text: Mass loading. A film on the path between the IDTs adds mass per unit area and slows the wave. With λ fixed,

answer: The shift follows mass per unit area: a mass sensitivity of 13.5 Hz per ng/cm² and a 7.4 µg/cm² film give 13.5 × 7400 = 99.9 kHz, consistent with the 100 kHz measured. Coating the path with antibodies makes an acoustic immunosensor; a soft film also adds attenuation, and temperature shifts v, so a reference delay line without the coating is used.

ISFET gate. An n-channel MOSFET with its metal gate removed: the gate insulator (SiO₂, better Si₃N₄, Al₂O₃ or Ta₂O₅) touches the solution, and a Ag/AgCl reference electrode in the solution sets the gate bias. Surface groups exchange H⁺ with the solution, so the surface charge and the threshold voltage follow pH: ΔVT = 2.303 (kT/q) ΔpH, ideally 59 mV per pH at 25 °C and 61.5 mV at 37 °C. It is a chemical (pH) sensor.

IMFET gate. An immunologically modified FET: an antibody (or antigen) layer is fixed on the ISFET gate. When the matching antigen binds, its charge changes the gate surface charge and shifts the threshold without any label. The signal is small and is screened by the ions of the solution within the Debye length, about a nanometre in physiological saline, so it works best in dilute buffer.

answer.text: ISFET against IMFET.

head: ISFET
IMFET
rows: a few mV, screened in salt

answer: Check. On a nitride ISFET at 37 °C with 90 % of the ideal slope, 0.90 × 61.5 = 55.4 mV per pH, so a blood pH fall from 7.40 to 7.30 lowers the threshold by 5.54 mV; the zirconia cell meanwhile gains 20.96 × ln 10 = 48.3 mV for each tenfold drop in sample oxygen.

bank.q: Design a finger-stick glucose biosensor: choose enzyme, mediator, electrode and readout, then explain how glucose concentration becomes a current.
outline: glucose oxidase or dehydrogenase as recognition enzyme
mediator or direct electron transfer
amperometric electrode and applied potential
current-to-concentration calibration and haematocrit error
answer: Specification. A single-use strip and a hand-held meter that read capillary blood glucose from 1.1 to 33 mmol/L (20 to 600 mg/dL) in about 5 s from under 1 µL of blood, with a result within about ±15 % of a laboratory method.

Enzyme. Glucose oxidase (GOx), with its FAD (flavin adenine dinucleotide) cofactor, is cheap, stable and specific to glucose: glucose + O₂ → gluconolactone + H₂O₂. FAD-dependent glucose dehydrogenase is an alternative that does not use oxygen at all, so the reading does not change with the blood oxygen level; it must be a type that ignores maltose and xylose.

Mediator. A first-generation design would oxidise H₂O₂ on platinum at +0.6 to +0.7 V, where ascorbic acid, uric acid and paracetamol also oxidise, and would depend on dissolved oxygen. A mediator such as ferricyanide (or a ferrocene or osmium complex) takes the electrons from the reduced FAD and carries them to the electrode at only +0.2 to +0.4 V, which removes most interference and the oxygen dependence. This is the second-generation design.

Electrodes. Screen-printed carbon (or sputtered gold or palladium) working and counter electrodes, and often a Ag/AgCl reference, on a plastic strip. The enzyme, mediator, a buffer and a wetting agent are dried over the working electrode. A capillary channel of fixed volume, under 1 µL, fills itself from the finger, and a fill-detect electrode tells the meter the channel is full.

Readout. The meter applies the fixed potential once the strip is full, waits a few seconds for the reaction, and measures the current (chronoamperometry) or the charge. A transimpedance amplifier turns the microampere current into a voltage, an ADC digitises it, and the microcontroller applies the strip-lot calibration code and a temperature correction before showing mmol/L or mg/dL.

answer.text: Glucose to current. Each glucose molecule gives two electrons to the electrode (via H₂O₂ or the mediator), so the charge is Q = 2 ng F. For a 0.6 µL sample at 5.5 mmol/L:

answer: Only the glucose near the electrode reacts in 5 s, so real currents are a few microamperes; what matters is that the current is proportional to glucose, and that proportionality is calibrated.

answer.text: Current to concentration. Two standards fix the line I = I₀ + S C. With 45 nA at 2.0 mmol/L and 165 nA at 10.0 mmol/L (scaled values for illustration):

answer: Haematocrit error. Red cells take up volume and slow diffusion in the capillary, so a high haematocrit (packed-cell volume) gives a low current and a low reading, and a low haematocrit a high reading. Meters correct it by measuring the strip's AC impedance, which depends on haematocrit, or by membranes that hold back cells. Other error sources are temperature, an under-filled strip, and expired enzyme.
Check. The normal fasting range of 3.9 to 5.5 mmol/L corresponds on this calibration to 15 + 15 × 3.9 = 73.5 nA up to 15 + 15 × 5.5 = 97.5 nA, so a 120 nA sample is correctly flagged as high.

bank.q: Select sensors for (a) CO in air, (b) pH of river water, (c) alcohol in breath. Justify the transducer and recognition or filter for each.
outline: CO: metal-oxide or electrochemical cell with filter
pH: glass electrode or ISFET
breath alcohol: fuel cell or semiconductor sensor
reasons for choice, cost and cross-sensitivity
answer: Approach. For each target choose a transducer that responds to it, a recognition or filter step that rejects what else is present, and check the range and the environment. Cost and maintenance decide between candidates.

(a) Carbon monoxide in air. Choice: an electrochemical CO cell. CO is oxidised at a catalytic working electrode (CO + H₂O → CO₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻) and oxygen is reduced at the counter electrode, so the cell is amperometric and its current is linear in CO concentration. It works at room temperature on microwatts, so a battery home alarm can run for years. A charcoal filter in front removes hydrogen sulphide and many organic vapours that would also react. A SnO₂ chemiresistor is the cheaper alternative, but it needs a 300 to 400 °C heater (tens to hundreds of milliwatts) and also responds to alcohol, LPG and humidity, so it gives more false alarms.

Number for (a). With a typical cell sensitivity of about 70 nA per ppm (a data-sheet figure, assumed here), the 50 ppm alarm level gives 50 × 70 = 3.5 µA, easily read by a transimpedance amplifier with Rf = 100 kΩ as 0.35 V.

(b) pH of river water. Choice: a combination glass electrode with a Ag/AgCl reference, read by a high-impedance pH meter, or a nitride-gate ISFET for a rugged field probe. The recognition is the glass (or nitride) surface, which exchanges only H⁺. River water is cool and of low ionic strength, so the meter needs temperature compensation and the reference junction must not clog with silt. An ISFET does not break and can be dried, but drifts and needs frequent calibration with pH 4 and pH 7 buffers.

Number for (b). The slope is 2.303 RT/F: at 25 °C, 59.2 mV per pH; in a river at 15 °C, 2.303 × 8.314 × 288.15 / 96 485 = 57.2 mV per pH. Using the 25 °C slope at 15 °C would make a reading 3 pH units from 7 (pH 4 or 10) wrong by 3 × (59.2 − 57.2)/57.2 ≈ 0.10 pH.

(c) Alcohol in breath. Choice: a fuel-cell sensor for an evidential or police tester. Ethanol in the breath is oxidised at a platinum electrode on a proton-conducting membrane; the charge passed is proportional to the ethanol in a fixed breath sample. It is specific to alcohols and does not respond to acetone from a diabetic's breath, unlike a SnO₂ sensor. A SnO₂ semiconductor sensor suits cheap personal testers but drifts, needs a heater and has cross-sensitivity. Infrared absorption near 3.4 µm or 9.5 µm is used in fixed evidential instruments.

answer.text: Number for (c). Breath alcohol is converted to blood alcohol with the 2100 : 1 partition ratio.
answer.pre:
limit 30 mg per 100 mL of blood = 0.30 g/L
breath equivalent = 0.30 g/L / 2100 = 0.143 mg of ethanol per litre of breath

answer.text: Summary.

answer: Cost and cross-sensitivity. The SnO₂ sensor is the cheapest in every case but the least selective; the electrochemical and fuel cells cost more and have a life of a few years because the electrolyte dries; the glass electrode is cheap but fragile.

Check. The three choices span the three electrochemical modes of the course: amperometric (CO cell), potentiometric (pH electrode) and amperometric charge counting (fuel cell); each converts 50 ppm CO, a 0.1 pH change or 0.143 mg/L of breath ethanol into a microampere current or a few millivolts.

bank.q: A piezoresistive pressure sensor has full-scale output 2.0 mV/V at 200 kPa and is supplied from 5 V. Find the bridge output at 80 kPa and state one reason the real output may differ.
outline: full-scale bridge output is 10 mV
linear ratio is 80/200 = 0.4
expected output is 4 mV
nonlinearity, temperature drift or mounting stress
answer: Data. Full-scale output 2.0 mV/V at 200 kPa; supply Vs = 5 V; applied pressure P = 80 kPa. The bridge output of a piezoresistive sensor is proportional to supply and, ideally, to pressure.
Step 1: full-scale output in volts. 2.0 mV/V × 5 V = 10.0 mV at 200 kPa.
Step 2: sensitivity per kPa. 10.0 mV / 200 kPa = 0.050 mV/kPa = 50 µV/kPa.
Step 3: fraction of full scale. 80 / 200 = 0.40.
Step 4: ideal output. Vo = 0.40 × 10.0 mV = 4.0 mV, or 80 kPa × 0.050 mV/kPa = 4.0 mV by the other route.

answer.text: Working table.

answer: Step 5: amplify for the ADC. A 0 to 5 V ADC needs a gain of 5 V / 10 mV = 500, so 80 kPa reads 4.0 mV × 500 = 2.0 V.

Why the real output may differ (any one, explained). (1) Zero offset: the four resistors are not perfectly matched, so the bridge gives a few hundred microvolts at zero pressure; an offset of 0.2 mV adds 5 % at 80 kPa unless it is subtracted. (2) Temperature: the span falls about 0.2 % per °C; 20 °C above the calibration temperature gives 4.0 × (1 − 0.002 × 20) = 3.84 mV. (3) Nonlinearity: the diaphragm stiffens at large deflection; a 0.25 % FS error is ±0.025 mV. (4) Supply change: the output is ratiometric, so a 4.9 V supply gives 4.0 × 4.9/5 = 3.92 mV unless the ADC uses the same supply as its reference. (5) Mounting stress from the package or a tight fitting adds a false strain and shifts the zero. (6) Hysteresis between rising and falling pressure.

Gauge or absolute. If the sensor is a gauge type, 80 kPa means 80 kPa above atmosphere; an absolute sensor at 80 kPa absolute would read below atmospheric pressure. Using the wrong reading type gives an error of about 101 kPa, larger than all the effects above.
Check. The output scales linearly: 200 kPa gives 10.0 mV, so 80 kPa, 40 % of the span, gives 40 % of 10.0 mV, which is 4.0 mV.

bank.q: Explain the process flow for a silicon diaphragm pressure sensor from wafer to packaged die: oxidation, masking, etching, bonding and metallization. Name one defect from each critical step.
outline: thermal oxidation and masking steps
anisotropic etch forms diaphragm or cavity
wafer bonding seals reference cavity
metallization and packaging defects such as pinholes or stress
answer: Target device. A 1000 µm square diaphragm, 20 µm thick, on a 525 µm (100) wafer, with four piezoresistors at its edges and a sealed vacuum reference cavity, giving an absolute pressure sensor.

answer.text: Process flow.

head: Step
What is done
Purpose
Typical defect
rows: RCA clean; thermal oxide grown at 900 to 1100 °C
insulation and a mask for implant
heavy boron diffusion or an SOI wafer sets the 20 µm diaphragm
lithography opens windows; boron implant forms the p-type resistors; anneal
misalignment puts gauges off the stress peak
open contact holes; sputter aluminium; pattern the bridge tracks
open or shorted tracks, high contact resistance
LPCVD nitride, patterned with front-to-back alignment
505 µm deep at 1.4 µm/min, about 361 min at 80 °C
glass to silicon at about 400 °C and several hundred volts, in vacuum
saw, die-attach, gold wire, gel or cap
package stress shifts the zero; moisture

answer: Oxidation. Thermal oxidation consumes silicon to grow a dense SiO2; it is growth, not deposition. It insulates the surface and masks the implant. A pinhole lets the implant or a later etch through and can short a resistor to the substrate.

Masking. Each lithography loop spins resist, exposes it through a mask aligned to the previous layer, develops it and transfers the pattern by etch or implant. This device needs about five masks (resistors, contacts, metal, back-side window, passivation). Misalignment, critical for the gauges, moves them away from the edge where the stress peaks and lowers the sensitivity.

answer.text: Anisotropic etching. KOH etches (100) silicon about 70 times faster than (111), so the pit walls are (111) planes at 54.74° and the pit narrows towards the front face. The back-side opening must allow for this:
answer.pre:
etch depth = 525 − 20 = 505 µm;  time = 505 / 1.4 = 360.7 min ≈ 6.0 h
run-out per side = 505 / tan 54.74° = 505 × 0.707 = 357 µm
mask opening = 1000 + 2 × 357 = 1714 µm

answer: The (111) walls themselves recede at about 0.02 µm/min, 7.2 µm over the 361 min, a small correction. A defect here is non-uniform depth across the wafer, which gives diaphragms of different thickness and therefore different spans; the boron or SOI etch stop exists to prevent it.

Bonding. Anodic bonding presses a sodium-containing glass (Pyrex type) to the silicon at about 400 °C with the glass several hundred volts negative; sodium ions drift away from the interface and the strong field pulls the surfaces into contact, forming a hermetic seal. Done in vacuum, it seals the reference cavity. Defects are voids from particles, leaks that let the reference pressure creep, and thermal-mismatch stress that shifts the zero.

Metallization. Sputtered aluminium, patterned into the bridge tracks and bond pads, and sintered to make ohmic contacts to the resistors. Defects are opens at steps, shorts from residues, and corrosion of aluminium in humid packages.

Check. The final die must be wider than the 1714 µm opening plus a rim for bonding, so it comes out about 2.5 mm across; the etch of about 6 h and the five masks are the main cost drivers, which is why DRIE (vertical walls, a 1000 µm opening) is used when dies must be smaller.

bank.q: Compare electrochemical, optical, acoustic and calorimetric biosensors on sensitivity, selectivity, cost and field use. Recommend one for a rural clinic and defend the choice.
outline: transduction mechanism of each class
sensitivity, selectivity and interference
cost, reagent needs and maintenance
clear recommendation with justification
answer: Electrochemical biosensors. The biological reaction makes or consumes an electroactive species or ions, and an electrode measures a current (amperometric), an EMF (potentiometric) or a conductance (conductometric). The glucose strip is the model: enzyme plus a mediator at +0.2 to +0.4 V, current linear in glucose. Worked value: with S = 15 nA per mmol/L and I₀ = 15 nA, a 120 nA reading is 7.0 mmol/L.

Optical biosensors. Binding or reaction changes absorbance, fluorescence or refractive index. Absorbance follows Beer-Lambert, A = ε c l; surface plasmon resonance (SPR) watches the angle of a reflectance dip on a gold film shift as antibodies capture antigen, label-free and in real time. Lateral-flow strips (pregnancy, malaria, COVID antigen) are the simplest optical immunosensors: gold nanoparticles make a coloured line read by eye.

Acoustic biosensors. An antibody-coated quartz crystal microbalance or SAW device shifts frequency as mass binds. Worked value: on a 100 MHz SAW line a mass sensitivity of 13.5 Hz per ng/cm² turns 7.4 µg/cm² into a 99.9 kHz shift. Label-free, but sensitive to temperature and to the viscosity of the liquid, so a reference line is needed.

Calorimetric biosensors. An enzyme column with a thermistor measures the heat of reaction. The rise is small: a thermistor with −4 %/K on 10 kΩ changes by only 10 000 × 0.04 × 0.001 = 0.4 Ω for 1 mK, so a bridge and careful thermal isolation are needed. Almost any enzyme reaction gives heat, so the method is general, but it is slow and bulky.

answer.text: Comparison.

head: Criterion
Electrochemical
Optical
Acoustic
Calorimetric
rows: very high for SPR and fluorescence (nmol/L and below); moderate for strips
from the enzyme; electroactive interferents at high potential
from the enzyme; any heat is read
very low (strip) to very high (SPR bench)
none for a strip; mains for SPR

answer: Sensitivity and interference. Optical methods reach the lowest concentrations, which is why SPR and fluorescence are laboratory research tools. Electrochemical sensors are sensitive enough for metabolites such as glucose, lactate and cholesterol, and the mediator keeps interference down. Acoustic sensors respond to anything that sticks to the surface, so blocking layers are needed against non-specific binding. Calorimetric sensors pick up every source of heat in the room.

Cost, reagents and maintenance. A glucose meter costs a few hundred rupees and its strips a few rupees to tens of rupees each; the strip carries dry reagents with a shelf life of months and needs no cold chain once sealed. A lateral-flow strip needs no instrument at all. SPR, SAW and calorimetric systems need mains power, temperature control, flowing buffers, coated chips and trained staff.

Recommendation for a rural clinic. Electrochemical sensors for quantitative metabolites (glucose, lactate, cholesterol), backed by optical lateral-flow strips for yes/no infection and pregnancy tests.

Defence of the choice. (1) The clinic needs quantitative glucose to manage diabetes, and only the electrochemical strip gives a number from one drop of blood on a battery meter. (2) Results come in seconds, so the patient is treated in one visit. (3) Strips and meters are cheap, robust, and need no cold chain once sealed, no water and no trained technician. (4) The weaknesses, strip shelf life, temperature and haematocrit errors, are handled by meters with built-in temperature and haematocrit correction, sealed strip vials and a control solution checked each week. (5) For infections, where a yes/no answer is enough, lateral-flow strips cost even less and need no power. Acoustic and calorimetric systems are rejected for cost, power and maintenance; SPR is a research instrument.

When the recommendation would change. If the clinic had to measure a protein marker at very low concentration, such as cardiac troponin, a hand-held fluorescence reader of immunoassay strips would be the better choice, still an optical method, and still battery-powered.

Check. Against the normal fasting range of 3.9 to 5.5 mmol/L, the electrochemical strip above gives 73.5 to 97.5 nA, so a 7.0 mmol/L sample at 120 nA stands 22.5 nA above the top of that band, a margin easily read by a pocket meter; the calorimetric sensor would have to read the same glucose as a fraction of a millikelvin.

bank.q: Evaluate a wearable patch that fuses a flexible temperature sensor with a flexible heart-rate sensor. Discuss drift, motion artefact, calibration and the benefit of fusion over one sensor.
outline: flexible sensor mounting and skin contact
drift and motion artefact in each channel
fusion rules or estimation
when fusion helps and when it can mislead
answer: The patch. A polyimide or PDMS patch on the chest carries a printed thermistor (or a printed silver or platinum RTD) for skin temperature, and a heart-rate channel: either printed dry Ag/AgCl ECG electrodes or an optical PPG (LED and photodiode). A small processor fuses the readings and sends them by Bluetooth.

Mounting and skin contact. The patch must follow the skin so that the sensors touch it. A thermistor reads skin temperature, which lies a few degrees below core temperature and changes with room air and sweating, so the patch needs a model (or a heat-flux sensor) to estimate core temperature. Dry ECG electrodes have a skin impedance of tens of kΩ at 10 Hz, so the amplifier needs a very high input impedance. Sweat under the film changes both channels.

Drift in each channel. Printed silver tracks oxidise and crack with repeated bending, so the thermistor or RTD resistance drifts and the temperature reading creeps; encapsulation (parylene or a laminated barrier) and periodic recalibration against a reference thermometer limit it. The ECG baseline wanders with electrode-skin potential and sweat; PPG amplitude drifts with skin perfusion and LED ageing, though heart rate (a timing measurement) is less affected than amplitude.

Motion artefact. Walking moves the electrodes and the skin, adding noise in the same 1 to 3 Hz band as the heartbeat. PPG is worst affected because pressure on the skin changes the blood volume under the sensor. An on-board accelerometer measures the motion so the processor can reject or subtract the corrupted segments.

Calibration. The temperature channel is calibrated at two points (for example 30 °C and 40 °C) against a reference and stored as offset and slope in the patch memory, as in a smart sensor. Heart rate needs no gain calibration but its error is estimated against a reference ECG at rest and while walking.

answer.text: Fusion rule. Two independent heart-rate estimates are combined by inverse-variance weighting, w = 1/σ². At rest the ECG gives 75 bpm with σ = 1.5 bpm and the PPG gives 72 bpm with σ = 3 bpm.

answer: The fused value lies close to the ECG and its spread, 1.34 bpm, is smaller than the ECG's 1.5 bpm. While walking, the accelerometer can raise the PPG's σ (say to 10 bpm) so its weight falls to 0.01 and the ECG dominates; a Kalman filter does this smoothly by tracking heart rate as a slowly changing state.

Fusion across temperature and heart rate. The two quantities are different, so they are fused at feature or decision level: a fever alarm is more credible when temperature rises and heart rate rises with it (about 10 bpm per °C in adults is a common rule), and a temperature jump with no heart-rate change during exercise is more likely a contact fault or sweat.

When fusion helps. When the errors are independent, the fused estimate is better than either sensor, gaps in one channel are covered by the other, and one failed sensor is detected because it disagrees.

When fusion can mislead. When the errors are correlated: a patch that lifts off the skin spoils both channels at once, and sweat affects both, so averaging gives a confident wrong answer and the 1/√N gain does not apply. Weights set at rest are wrong during exercise. Fusion also hides a slowly drifting channel unless each channel is checked against its own limits.

Check. With equal σ of 1.5 bpm on both channels, fusion would give 1.5 / √2 = 1.06 bpm; with the PPG at 3 bpm the gain is smaller (1.34 bpm), because the better channel already carries 0.444 / 0.556 = 80 % of the weight.

glossary.def: A device that turns the concentration of a chemical species into an electrical signal through a recognition layer and a transducer.
A sensor that uses a biological recognition element to detect an analyte and a transducer to produce the electrical output.
The target substance whose concentration or activity is being measured.
The biological part of a biosensor, such as an enzyme, antibody, DNA strand or whole cell, that binds or reacts with the analyte.
An electrochemical sensor that measures an equilibrium EMF at almost zero current and relates it to ion activity.
An electrochemical sensor that applies a fixed potential and measures the current produced by oxidation or reduction of the analyte.
A sensor that measures the change in electrical conductance of a solution or film caused by the analyte.
A biosensor in which an enzyme converts the target into a product that the transducer can measure.
A biosensor that uses an antibody-antigen binding reaction and a transducer to detect the bound antigen or antibody.
A biosensor that uses whole microbial cells as the recognition element, often through their respiration or metabolite production.
A resistor, usually a metal-oxide film, whose resistance changes when a gas is adsorbed on its surface.
A gas sensor that measures heat released when a combustible gas burns on a catalytic bead.
The percentage ratio of actual water-vapour pressure to saturation water-vapour pressure at the same temperature.
The temperature at which air at a given moisture content becomes saturated and condensation begins.
The change in electrical resistance of a material when it is mechanically strained.
Microelectromechanical systems, small devices made by micromachining that combine mechanical parts with electrical circuits.
A fabrication method that etches deep into a silicon wafer to create cavities, diaphragms, beams or channels.
A fabrication method that builds thin movable structures by depositing and then removing sacrificial layers on a wafer surface.
A sensor package that includes signal conditioning, processing and a digital interface so it gives calibrated and addressed output.
The combination of readings from several sensors to produce an estimate that is better than any single reading.
A sensor made on a bendable substrate so that it can conform to skin, fabric or a curved surface.
An ionic conductor that carries one type of ion through its crystal lattice and is used in electrochemical cells.
A piezoelectric device in which a surface acoustic wave changes velocity or amplitude when mass or elasticity changes on the surface.
An ion-sensitive field-effect transistor whose drain current depends on the ion activity at its exposed gate insulator.
An immunologically modified field-effect transistor that places an antibody or antigen layer on the gate of a FET biosensor.
A disposable amperometric test strip with glucose oxidase and a mediator, used in blood glucose meters.
Immunologically modified FET: an ISFET whose gate carries an antibody or antigen layer, so binding shifts the threshold voltage.
Enzyme FET: an ISFET under an enzyme layer; the enzyme reaction changes the local pH, which the ISFET reads.
Flavin adenine dinucleotide, the cofactor of glucose oxidase that takes the electrons from glucose.
A redox molecule such as ferricyanide or ferrocene that carries electrons from an enzyme to the electrode at a low potential.
An amperometric oxygen electrode: a platinum cathode behind an oxygen-permeable membrane, used for blood pO₂.
The fraction of blood volume taken by red cells; it changes the reading of glucose strips.
